chapter_theme: Under the heading சான்றோர் செய்கை, nine verses on how the worthy act: they keep up ஒப்புரவு in want, even by borrowing, speak truth though beholden, do not cast off those they took in or friends who prove faulty, pity an enemy in distress, and, though great by birth, depend on and keep company with the lesser; their poverty outranks the wealth of the small.

81.reading: The worthy man born into a house that practises ஒப்புரவு goes on doing it even when he has no earned wealth, and though no one tends him and he grazes where there is no grass, he grows into what his house is, as a bull's calf becomes a bull.
81.nuance: The proverb puts the weight on birth over nurture: the calf is neither cared for nor fed and still becomes a bull. The verse does not say the man earns again; it says the habit of the house survives the loss of the means.

pazhamozhi.literal: a bull's calf turns into a bull

story.act: no story; the proverb is applied to the man of a giving house who is poor and untended

pazhamozhi.applied_to: the habit of helping others, inherited from the house, outlasts poverty and neglect

82.reading: Even when they are crushed into want and cannot manage, the worthy do not sit back thinking they will see to it when a chance comes; they do what is due even if they must borrow to do it.
82.nuance: The proverb turns on கடன், which is both debt and duty: the worthy take on a debt (கடங்கொண்டும்) to pay a duty (கடன்). Line 2 names the excuse they refuse, putting off the act until a better time.

pazhamozhi.literal: the worthy will do their duty even by taking a loan

story.act: no story; the proverb is applied to the worthy man in want

pazhamozhi.applied_to: want is no ground for postponing what one owes others

83.reading: The verse asks what can be said for those who, in a crowded battle, carry the enemy's lies in their mouths and go over in treachery, and answers that the worthy speak the truth even when they have eaten from another's hand.
83.nuance: கையுண்டும் most plausibly means having eaten at someone's hand, that is, being beholden to him, so the worthy are not bought by what they have received; it could also be read as having taken something into the hand, a bribe. Lines 1 and 2 are compressed and the sense of அறைபோய் as going over in treachery is a reading.
83.domain_note: men serving in war, set against traitors

pazhamozhi.literal: the worthy speak the truth even after eating from someone's hand

story.act: no story; the proverb is set against the traitor in battle who repeats the enemy's lie

pazhamozhi.applied_to: being beholden does not bend the worthy man's truth, as it bends the traitor's

84.reading: The verse says there is no question of 'there' or 'here': those who have taken in people who came to them do not then cast them off as worthless, any more than anyone who has strapped on a drum has gone away without beating it.
84.nuance: The argument rests on a commitment once taken up: the drum, once worn, is beaten. Lines 1 and 2 are a rhetorical question whose subject is unstated, and ஆண்டீண்டு may mean 'in this place or that' or 'this world or the next'; the reading takes மாண்டிலார் as 'people without worth', the excuse for disowning.

pazhamozhi.literal: no one who put on a drum has gone off without beating it

story.act: no story; the proverb is applied to one who has taken in those who sought him

pazhamozhi.applied_to: a protection once given is not withdrawn by calling the protected unworthy

85.reading: The worthy do not turn against those they have cherished even if those people lack good qualities, for feeding the friends one made in the sight of the whole village is a duty.
85.nuance: The proverb makes the bond public: the friendship was made where the village could see (ஊரறிய), so dropping it would break a pledge others witnessed, not only a private feeling. The verse grants the friends' faults outright.

pazhamozhi.literal: is it not a duty to feed those one befriended before the village

story.act: no story; the proverb is applied to the worthy man whose friends prove of poor character

pazhamozhi.applied_to: a friendship made openly binds even when the friend proves unworthy

86.reading: When the better sort see a plain enemy in distress they still show him kindly regard, even if he is of a kind that does harm, for a snake brought into the assembly of the worthy does not die.
86.nuance: The case is the hardest one: the enemy is open (தெற்றப் பகைவர்) and still dangerous (நவைக்கப் படுந்தன்மைத்து), and the moment is his weakness, when killing him would be easy. The snake is the image for such a man.

pazhamozhi.literal: a snake that comes before the assembly of the worthy does not die

story.act: no story; the proverb is applied to the dangerous enemy who falls into the good man's power

pazhamozhi.applied_to: the worthy spare and pity even a harmful enemy in distress

87.reading: The verse says those far above others by birth, not thinking it too great a lowering, go to those small by birth and live in reliance on them, like a தால shelter.
87.nuance: பிறப்பிற் சிறியார் and பிறப்பினால் மிக்கவர் rank people by birth; the verse takes the ranking as given and praises the high-born for setting it aside when they need shelter. The proverb is obscure: தாலம் may be the palmyra, a plate, or the earth, and I cannot fix what a தால அடைக்கலம் was. Whether the verse praises humility or reports necessity is read from the heading.

norm.note: a birth-rank of the period: people ranked as great or small by birth, taken as given

pazhamozhi.literal: like a தால refuge (sense not fixed)

story.act: no story; the proverb is applied to the high-born who take refuge with the low-born

pazhamozhi.applied_to: the high-born are not shamed by depending on those below them by birth

88.reading: The verse says that when those born in great families conduct themselves as kin with those lesser than they, it is the way the string is joined to the flower.
88.nuance: The image leaves the gain mostly with the lesser party, the string that is carried with the flower, though the garland needs both. The phrase சிறியார் இனமாய் ஒழுகுதல் could also be read the other way, the lesser keeping company as kin of the great; the reading follows the heading. குடி here ranks families by birth.

norm.note: family rank of the period: great and small houses ranked by birth, taken as given

pazhamozhi.literal: the way string is joined with flowers

story.act: no story; the proverb is applied to great families who take lesser people into their company

pazhamozhi.applied_to: the great raise the lesser by joining them, as a flower lends itself to its string

89.reading: The poverty of the great is better than the wealth the small have come by, which is a thing to be ashamed of, for old ghee never becomes worse than buttermilk.
89.nuance: The proverb concedes that the ghee is old, that is, that the great have declined, and holds that what they are still ranks above the fresh but lesser thing. நாண attaches shame to the small men's wealth, not to the poverty.

pazhamozhi.literal: old ghee is never worse than buttermilk

story.act: no story; the proverb is applied to the great man fallen poor beside the small man grown rich

pazhamozhi.applied_to: the declined worth of the great still outranks the wealth of the small

links.note: Kural 955 says an old family does not part from its nature when what it can give has shrunk; Pazhamozhi 81 says a man of a giving house keeps up ஒப்புரவு without wealth, and adds that he does so though untended and unfed.
links.teaches: The Kural treats the shrunken means as the only test; Pazhamozhi adds neglect, so the inherited nature is shown to hold without either resources or nurture.
links.list_adds: its proverb of the unfed calf that still becomes a bull makes the claim one of nature against upbringing, which the couplet does not raise.

links.note: Both use grass and a beast to show that the well-born keep their nature in hardship: the lion will not chew creeping grass, the bull's calf grows into a bull though it grazes where there is no grass.
links.teaches: The same pasture image argues in two directions: the Naladiyar's lion refuses what is beneath it, while Pazhamozhi's calf needs nothing from the pasture at all, so lineage is shown both as refusal and as self-sufficient growth.
links.list_adds: it turns the image from what the well-born will not do to what they become regardless, and ties it to the act of ஒப்புரவு rather than to principle in general.

links.note: Kural 220 says ruin through ஒப்புரவு is worth buying even by selling oneself; Pazhamozhi 82 names the concrete form of that cost, borrowing to do what is due, and the excuse it refuses, waiting for a better time.
links.teaches: Read together they show the Kural's startling price, selling oneself, as the far end of an ordinary practice the worthy actually follow: going into debt rather than postponing a duty.
links.list_adds: its pun on கடன் as debt and duty makes the cost and the obligation one word, which the couplet keeps as ruin set against gain.

links.note: Naladiyar 80 forbids eating from the hands of those one should not eat from and speaking words mixed with falsehood; Pazhamozhi 83 grants that the worthy may have eaten from another's hand and says they speak the truth even so.
links.teaches: The Naladiyar guards truth by refusing the obligation that might bend it; Pazhamozhi allows the obligation and makes truth hold against it, a stronger and riskier claim.
links.list_adds: it sets the worthy man's truth beside the traitor's borrowed lie in battle, a contrast of two men under obligation that the quatrain's separate refusals lack.

links.note: Both proverbs rest on a public commitment: the man who strapped on the drum beats it, the man who made friends before the village feeds them; 84 applies this to those who came for shelter, 85 to friends who prove faulty.
links.teaches: Taken together the two verses ground loyalty not in the worth of the person protected but in the protector's own visible pledge, so the other's unworthiness is ruled out twice as an excuse.

links.note: Purananuru 203 tells a king that refusing a returning suppliant with 'you took before' is cruel and that protecting suppliants is his duty; Pazhamozhi 84 says those who took in seekers do not cast them off as worthless.
links.teaches: The puram poem closes the excuse of past giving and the ethics verse closes the excuse of the seeker's unworthiness, so together they show the protector's duty answering two different pretexts for withdrawal.

links.note: Kural 806 says those who keep within bounds do not give up an old friendship even when it brings ruin; Pazhamozhi 85 says the worthy do not change toward cherished friends who lack good qualities, because the friendship was made before the village.
links.teaches: The Kural makes constancy a mark of the man who keeps bounds; Pazhamozhi adds a reason outside him, the village that witnessed the bond, so loyalty becomes a public obligation as well as a private virtue.
links.list_adds: its proverb names the friend's bad character outright and answers it with feeding as a duty, a concrete act the couplet does not specify.

links.note: Kural 579 ranks highest the disposition to show kindly regard and bear with those whose way is to hurt; Pazhamozhi 86 sets that regard at one moment, when an open and dangerous enemy is in distress.
links.teaches: The pairing fixes when the Kural's demand is hardest: not under the enemy's attack but at his fall, when sparing him is a choice and he may still bite.
links.list_adds: the snake proverb names the enemy as still dangerous and the assembly of the worthy as the place he is spared, a setting and a risk the couplet leaves out.

links.note: Both verses set the high-born beside those small by birth: in 87 the great go to the small and depend on them, in 88 the great take the small into their company.
links.teaches: Read together they show the edition's heading praising the great for crossing the birth-rank in both directions, as dependents and as patrons, while leaving the ranking itself in place.

links.note: Kural 451 says greatness fears small company and only smallness takes it as kin; Pazhamozhi 88 praises great families who conduct themselves as kin with those lesser than they. The conflict holds on the reading that 88's சிறியார் are the same small people the Kural warns against, not merely those of lower rank.
links.teaches: The two split on whether keeping company with the lesser degrades the great or raises the lesser: the Kural fears contamination, Pazhamozhi sees the flower lending itself to the string.
links.list_adds: its proverb reverses the direction of influence that the couplet assumes, making the great the ones who pass on their quality.

links.note: Kural 960 says one who wants lineage must want humility toward all; Pazhamozhi 88 shows the great families in the act, keeping kin-like company with those below them.
links.teaches: The Kural states humility as the condition of lineage; Pazhamozhi gives its form and its effect, the lesser carried along like string with the flower.
links.list_adds: it turns the couplet's general humility into one practice, keeping the lesser as kin, and adds what the lesser gain from it.

links.note: Kural 657 sets the utter poverty of the worthy above wealth gained under blame; Pazhamozhi 89 sets the poverty of the great above the wealth the small have reached, calling that wealth shameful.
links.teaches: The Kural condemns wealth for how it was got; Pazhamozhi condemns it for who holds it, so the pair shows two grounds on which wealth can rank below poverty.
links.list_adds: the old-ghee proverb concedes the great man's decline and ranks him above the fresh lesser thing anyway, a turn the couplet's plain ranking lacks.

links.note: Both rank the poverty of the worthy above others' wealth through an image of what is drunk or eaten: the Naladiyar's small well beside the sea, Pazhamozhi's old ghee beside buttermilk.
links.teaches: The images argue differently for the same ranking: the Naladiyar's well is preferred because it can be used, Pazhamozhi's ghee because its kind does not change with age, so one rests the claim on use and the other on nature.
links.list_adds: it measures the worthy against the small rather than against those ignorant of the next world, making the ranking one of character rather than of foresight.

source_issues: 87: the proverb தால அடைக்கலமே போன்று is obscure as printed; தால may be corrupt, and the sense of the closing image cannot be fixed from the text.
